readingInstruction: Read Isaiah 54:1-57:21. After the cross of chapter 53 comes the fruit: a barren woman sings, the covenant is widened, and everyone who thirsts is invited to come. Read Isaiah 55 slowly.
settingTheScene: Chapter 54 follows directly from the Servant’s death. Because the Servant gave himself, Zion, a woman barren and desolate, will have many children. The following chapters broaden the invitation. The gate is opened to foreigners and eunuchs who were once excluded. The covenant now rests on grace. And the section ends with a warning that there is no peace for the wicked.
observation: “Sing, O barren one, who did not bear; break forth into singing and cry aloud” (54:1).
“For a brief moment I deserted you, but with great compassion I will gather you” (54:7).
“For the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but my steadfast love shall not depart from you” (54:10).
“No weapon that is fashioned against you shall succeed” (54:17).
“Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat!” (55:1).
“Seek the LORD while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (55:6).
“For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares the LORD” (55:8).
“So shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty” (55:11).
interpretation:
The command to sing in chapter 54 is startling. The one addressed is a barren woman, and yet she is told to sing, for the children of the desolate will be more than those of the married. The cross has made this possible. Because the Servant was cut off from the land of the living, many are born. The promises that follow are tender. God is her husband, her redeemer. He admits that for a moment he forsook her in his anger, but with everlasting love he has compassion. And he swears, as in the days of Noah, that he will not be angry with her again. The mountains may depart, but his love will not.

Chapter 55 is one of the greatest invitations in the Bible. “Come, everyone who thirsts.” It is free: “He who has no money, come, buy and eat… without money and without price.” The paradox of buying without money states the nature of grace. The question: “Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy?” It describes the empty pursuits of the world. God offers an everlasting covenant, the “sure mercies of David,” now extended to all.

The call is urgent: “Seek the LORD while he may be found.” It includes a call to repentance: “Let the wicked forsake his way… let him return to the LORD, that he may have compassion on him, and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.” The reason for confidence is that God’s ways are higher than ours: “As the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways.” This is not a statement of distance but of generosity. His pardon is greater than we think possible. And his word is effective, like rain that waters the earth. It does not return empty.

Chapter 56 is a surprising word of inclusion. Foreigners and eunuchs, who were barred from the assembly in the law, are welcomed. “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.” Chapter 57 then contrasts the contrite and humble, with whom God dwells, to the wicked, who have no peace.
connection: Jesus said, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37) and to the woman at the well offered living water (John 4:10-14). Revelation 22:17 invites, “Let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price.” Jesus quoted Isaiah 56:7 when he cleansed the temple (Mark 11:17). Galatians 4:27 quotes Isaiah 54:1. Acts 13:34 quotes “the sure mercies of David” as fulfilled in Christ’s resurrection. Matthew 5:3 echoes “the poor in spirit” of Isaiah 57:15.
application:
Accept Isaiah 55:1 as an invitation. What are you spending on “that which is not bread”? Bring that thirst to God.

Welcome someone who has been left out of your circle, as God welcomed the foreigner and the eunuch.

Trust the word you read, as rain that waters the earth and will not return empty.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you are thirsty for.
Confess where you have spent your labor on what does not satisfy.
Ask him to help you seek him while he may be found.
